summary: This work systematically characterizes NbTiN superconducting spiral inductors under elevated temperatures (2–8 K) and magnetic fields (up to 750 mT) relevant for spin-qubit RF reflectometry. By combining weakly coupled resonator measurements with independent two-port inductance extraction, the authors show that temperature- and field-dependent frequency shifts are primarily inductive in origin and can be reconstructed from kinetic-inductance changes alone.
motivation: Scalable spin-qubit architectures require RF reflectometry circuits operating at temperatures above 1 K and magnetic fields of several hundred millitesla to enable on-chip cryogenic integration, but performance degradation of superconducting circuit elements under these conditions remains poorly understood.
method: Six NbTiN spiral inductors (geometric inductances 47–176 nH, kinetic-inductance fractions $\alpha = 5–9\%$) were fabricated and characterized using two complementary setups: weakly coupled notch-resonator measurements extracting $f_0$ and $Q_i$, and wire-bonded two-port measurements extracting inductance $L$. Temperature and field dependencies were modeled using BCS gap theory for kinetic inductance and vortex-penetration physics.
result: Measured $L(T)$ and $f_0(T)$ are consistent with quasiparticle-driven kinetic-inductance changes ($\Delta L_k/L_k \approx 20\%$ from 2–8 K); frequency shifts remain below 1%. Quality factors degrade above a device-dependent field threshold $B_Q$ (300–391 mT for in-plane field) due to vortex losses at strip edges, with $B_Q \propto 1/w$ scaling. At $T = 2$ K and $B = 0$, devices achieve $Q_i \approx (3–4) \times 10^4$, with temperature-dependent loss modeled by activated quasiparticle generation ($Q_{\mathrm{other}} = 2.8 \times 10^4$).
